description: A man walked along the beach early in the morning.
text:
A man walked along the beach early in the morning. The night before, a big storm came. Now thousands of starfish lay on the sand. They could not go back to the sea.

He saw a little girl. She picked up a starfish and threw it into the water. Then she picked up another one and did the same.

“What are you doing?” asked the man. “There are thousands of starfish. You cannot save them all. It doesn’t matter.”

The girl listened. She bent down, took another starfish, and threw it into the sea.

“It matters to this one,” she said.

The man was quiet. He thought about her words. Then he bent down and picked up a starfish too. He threw it into the water.

Soon, they worked together. Many people came and helped them.

By the end of the day, thousands of starfish were back in the sea.

Moral: You cannot help everyone, but you can help someone.

title: Stone Soup
description: A hungry traveler came to a small village.
text:
A hungry traveler came to a small village. He knocked on many doors. “Please, can you give me some food?” he asked.

“No,” said everyone. “We have nothing.”

The traveler smiled. He took a big pot and filled it with water. He put a stone in it and made a fire.

A woman came out. “What are you making?” she asked.

“Stone soup,” said the man. “It is delicious. But it needs a little salt.”

The woman brought some salt. Then a man came and asked, “What is that?” The traveler said, “Stone soup! It needs a carrot.” The man brought carrots.

Soon, other people brought potatoes, onions, and meat. Everyone helped a little.

At last, the soup was ready. It smelled wonderful. All the villagers sat together and ate. It was the best soup they ever tasted.

“Thank you,” said the villagers. “We learned something today. When we share, everyone has enough.”

The traveler smiled and took his stone.

Moral: When people share, there is enough for everybody.

title: The Fox and the Grapes
description: One hot day, a hungry fox walked in the forest.
text:
One hot day, a hungry fox walked in the forest. He was thirsty and tired.

Suddenly, he saw a vine. Big, purple grapes hung from a high branch. They looked sweet and juicy.

“Yummy!” said the fox. “I want those grapes.”

He jumped, but he could not reach them. He jumped again and again. Still, the grapes were too high.

He tried to climb the tree, but he fell. He tried running and jumping, but it did not work. After many tries, the fox was very tired.

He sat down and looked at the grapes. “Oh well,” he said. “I don’t want those grapes. They are probably sour anyway.”

He walked away with his nose in the air.

A little bird saw everything. She laughed and said, “He wanted the grapes very much. But he said bad things about them because he could not get them.”

Moral: Some people say bad things about what they cannot have.

title: The Goose with the Golden Eggs
description: A poor farmer had a goose.
text:
A poor farmer had a goose. One morning, he found a shiny egg in her nest. It was made of gold!

The farmer sold the egg and bought food and clothes. The next day, the goose laid another golden egg. Every day there was a new one.

Soon, the farmer was rich. But he wanted more. “One egg a day is too slow,” he thought. “Inside the goose, there must be many eggs. I will take them all today!”

He took a knife and cut open the goose. But inside, there was nothing. There were no golden eggs, only a normal goose.

The goose died. The farmer cried. “What did I do?” he said. “I was greedy, and now I have lost everything.”

There were no more golden eggs. The farmer became poor again, and he was very sad.

Moral: Don’t be greedy. If you want everything at once, you can lose everything.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
description: In summer, the sun was hot and the fields were green.
text:
In summer, the sun was hot and the fields were green. A grasshopper played music and sang all day.

An ant walked past. She carried a big piece of corn.

“Why do you work so hard?” asked the grasshopper. “Come and play with me!”

“I am getting food for winter,” said the ant. “You should do it too.”

The grasshopper laughed. “Winter is far away. Today is a good day!” He kept singing.

The ant worked every day. She carried food to her home and stored it safely.

Then winter came. It was cold, and snow covered everything. The grasshopper had no food and no house. He was hungry and cold.

He went to the ant’s door. “Please, can you give me some food?” he asked.

The ant looked at him kindly. “You played all summer,” she said. “But I will help you this time. Next summer, please prepare.”

The grasshopper ate and felt warm. He learned his lesson.

Moral: Work today, and tomorrow will be easier.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
description: A big lion was sleeping under a tree.
text:
A big lion was sleeping under a tree. A small mouse ran over his nose. The lion woke up and was very angry. He caught the mouse with his big paw.

“Please let me go,” said the mouse. “One day, I will help you.”

The lion laughed. “You? You are too small to help me!” But he let the mouse go.

A few days later, hunters came to the forest. They caught the lion in a strong net. The lion shouted loudly, but he could not get out.

The little mouse heard him and came quickly. “Don’t worry,” he said. “I will help you.”

The mouse used his small teeth. He cut the ropes one by one. Soon, the net was open, and the lion was free.

“Thank you, my friend,” said the lion. “I was wrong. Small friends can be great friends.”

The mouse smiled. From that day, the lion and the mouse were good friends.

Moral: Nobody is too small to help.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
description: A hare was very fast.
text:
A hare was very fast. He always laughed at a slow tortoise. “You are so slow!” he said.

The tortoise smiled. “Let’s have a race,” he said.

The hare laughed. “Okay!”

All the animals came to watch. The race began. The hare ran very fast and soon he could not see the tortoise.

“This is easy,” said the hare. “I can sleep now.” He lay under a tree and closed his eyes.

The tortoise did not stop. He walked slowly, step by step. He walked and walked.

The sun went down. The tortoise passed the sleeping hare. He kept going.

Finally, the hare woke up. He looked around. “Where is the tortoise?” he asked. Then he saw him near the end of the road!

The hare ran as fast as he could, but it was too late. The tortoise crossed the line first.

All the animals shouted, “The tortoise wins!”

The hare felt ashamed. He said, “You are slow, but you never stopped.”

Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
description: A boy looked after sheep on a hill near his village.
text:
A boy looked after sheep on a hill near his village. Every day was the same, and he was bored.

One day, he had an idea. He shouted, “Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is eating the sheep!”

The villagers heard him. They ran up the hill with sticks. But there was no wolf. The boy laughed. “I’m joking!” he said. The villagers were angry and went home.

A few days later, the boy did it again. “Wolf! Wolf!” he shouted. The villagers ran up the hill again. Again, there was no wolf. The boy laughed, and the villagers were very angry.

Then, one evening, a real wolf came. The boy was afraid. He shouted, “Wolf! Wolf! Please help me!”

The villagers heard him, but they said, “He is joking again.” Nobody came.

The wolf ate many sheep. The boy sat on the hill and cried.

Later, he told an old man, “I told the truth this time. Why did nobody help me?”

The old man said, “Because you lied before. Now nobody believes you.”

Moral: If you lie, people will not trust you, even when you tell the truth.

title: The Magic Backpack
description: Sam was a boy who forgot everything.
text:
Sam was a boy who forgot everything. He forgot his homework, his lunch, and even his shoes. His mother was always worried.

One day, his grandfather gave him an old backpack. “This is a magic backpack,” he said. “But it only works if you follow three rules. Every evening, put your things inside. Check the list. And go to bed early.”

Sam laughed. “A magic backpack? Okay!”

That evening, he put his books, his lunch, and his homework into the bag. He checked the list on his door. Then he went to bed early.

The next morning, everything was ready. He did not forget anything. At school, the teacher said, “Wonderful, Sam! You have all your homework today!”

Sam did the same thing every day. After a month, he did not need the list anymore. Good habits became natural.

He told his grandfather, “The backpack is truly magic!”

His grandfather laughed. “The bag is old, my boy. It was never magic. The magic was in you. You made a good habit.”

Sam smiled. He understood.

Moral: Small good habits can change your life.

title: The Smart Little Girl
description: A king was walking in his garden when he met a little girl who was selling flowers.
text:
A king was walking in his garden when he met a little girl who was selling flowers.

“What do you have there?” asked the king.

“Flowers, Your Majesty,” said the girl. “They are one coin each.”

The king wanted to test her. “I will give you one coin,” he said, “but tell me: where does the sun go at night?”

“It goes to the same place where it was before, Your Majesty,” said the girl. “It is always shining somewhere.”

The king was surprised. “Very good! Now, tell me: how many stars are in the sky?”

“As many as the hairs on your head,” said the girl. “If you don’t believe me, you can count them.”

The king laughed loudly. “You are clever!” he said. “What do you want as a reward?”

The girl thought. “I don’t want gold,” she said. “I want to go to school. I want to learn many things.”

The king smiled. He sent her to the best school in the country. Many years later, she became a wise advisor to the king.

Moral: Knowledge is more valuable than gold.

title: The Fisherman and the Businessman
description: A businessman walked along a beach.
text:
A businessman walked along a beach. He saw a fisherman lying next to his small boat, enjoying the sun.

“Why aren’t you fishing?” asked the businessman.

“I fished this morning,” said the fisherman. “I caught enough for my family.”

“But you could fish more!” said the businessman. “Then you could sell the fish and buy a bigger boat. After that, you could buy many boats and start a big company.”

“And then?” asked the fisherman.

“Then you could become rich and famous,” said the businessman. “In twenty years, you can stop working and relax.”

The fisherman smiled. “And what will I do when I stop working?”

“You can go to the beach,” said the businessman. “You can fish a little, play with your children, and rest in the sun!”

The fisherman laughed. “But that is what I’m doing right now.”

The businessman opened his mouth, but he had no answer. He looked at the sea for a long time and then walked away slowly, thinking.

Moral: Don’t wait for happiness. It may be right in front of you.

title: The Boy Who Planted Seeds
description: A little boy named Ben lived in a big city.
text:
A little boy named Ben lived in a big city. His street was gray and dirty. There were no trees and no flowers. Ben was sad about it.

One day, he found some flower seeds in his grandmother’s kitchen. “I will plant these,” he thought. He went outside and put the seeds in the ground near his house.

Every day, he gave them water. Some neighbors laughed. “Nothing will grow in this dirty place,” they said. But Ben did not stop.

After three weeks, little green leaves came out of the ground. After one month, there were red and yellow flowers. They looked beautiful against the gray wall.

People stopped to look at them. “How lovely!” they said. A girl asked, “Can I plant some too?” Ben gave her a few seeds.

Soon, other children began to plant flowers. Then the adults joined them. Little by little, the whole street changed. It had flowers, small trees, and green plants everywhere.

A year later, the street was the most beautiful place in the city. And it all began with one boy and a few seeds.

Moral: One small action can change a whole place.

title: The Three Questions
description: A wise man lived in a small town.
text:
A wise man lived in a small town. One day, a man ran up to him. “Teacher, I have something to tell you about your friend!” he said excitedly.

“Wait,” said the wise man. “Before you speak, let’s use the three questions. Is it true?”

The man thought. “Well... I heard it from someone. I’m not sure.”

“Is it good?” asked the wise man.

“No,” said the man. “It is bad news.”

“Is it useful?” asked the wise man. “Will it help me or my friend?”

The man was quiet. “No, I don’t think so.”

The wise man smiled. “If it is not true, not good, and not useful, why do you want to tell it to me?”

The man felt ashamed and went home. He understood that talking about other people can hurt them.

After that, he thought about these three questions before he spoke. And he never gossiped again. People in the town liked him more because he spoke only kind and useful words.

Moral: Before you speak, ask yourself: Is it true, is it kind, is it useful?

title: The Boy and the Nails
description: There was a boy with a very bad temper.
text:
There was a boy with a very bad temper. When he was angry, he shouted and said unkind words to other people. His father was worried.

One day, the father gave him a bag of nails. “Every time you lose your temper,” he said, “hit one nail into the wooden fence.”

On the first day, the boy hit thirty-seven nails into the fence. Over the next weeks, he learned to control himself. Each day, he hit fewer nails. It was easier to stay calm than to hit nails.

At last, there was a day when the boy did not hit any nail. He told his father proudly.

“Good!” said his father. “Now, every day that you stay calm, pull out one nail.”

Many weeks passed. At last, all the nails were gone. The father took his son to the fence. “You did well,” he said. “But look at the holes. The fence will never be the same. Angry words are like these nails. You can say sorry, but the hole is still there.”

The boy looked at the fence and was silent. He never forgot that lesson.

Moral: Angry words leave scars, so think before you speak.

title: The Lazy Donkey
description: A merchant had a donkey.
text:
A merchant had a donkey. Every day, he loaded it with heavy bags of salt and walked to the market. The road was long, and there was a river on the way.

One day, the donkey slipped in the river. The bags fell into the water, and the salt became light. When the donkey stood up, the bags were much lighter. “How wonderful!” he thought.

After that, the lazy donkey fell into the river every day on purpose. Every time, the salt melted, and his work became easier.

The merchant saw it and understood. “I will teach you a lesson,” he thought.

The next day, he put bags of cotton on the donkey’s back. The donkey walked to the river and fell down again, thinking, “Now my bags will be light.”

But this time, the cotton became wet and very heavy. The donkey could hardly stand. He walked slowly and painfully all the way to the market.

After that day, the donkey never played tricks again. He worked honestly.

Moral: Tricks and laziness sometimes bring more trouble.

title: The Teacher's Test
description: A teacher gave her class a test.
text:
A teacher gave her class a test. Before it started, she said, “Please read all the questions first, and then begin.”

The students started reading. The test had one hundred questions. Many of the questions were very difficult. “Oh no,” whispered the students. They began to write very quickly.

One student, Maria, read the whole test carefully before she started. At the end of the page, she saw something. It said: “Do not answer any questions. Just write your name at the top of the paper and give it back to your teacher.”

Maria smiled. She wrote her name and gave the paper to the teacher.

After twenty minutes, the other students were still writing. They were sweating and worried. At last, the teacher said, “Time is up. Please stop.”

She looked at the class. “I asked you to read all the questions first,” she said. “Only Maria did. The test was not about the answers. It was about listening.”

The students laughed and felt embarrassed. They understood.

Moral: Listen carefully and read instructions before you act.

title: The Mango Tree
description: In a small village, there was an old mango tree.
text:
In a small village, there was an old mango tree. It was very big and gave sweet fruit every summer. All the children loved it.

A little boy named Ravi came to the tree every day. He climbed it, ate mangoes, and slept in the shade. The tree was very happy.

Years passed. Ravi became a teenager. He did not come every day. One day, he came and said, “I need money. I have no toys.”

“Take my mangoes and sell them,” said the tree. Ravi sold them and was happy.

Later, Ravi became a man. He came and said, “I need a house for my family.”

“Cut my branches and build your house,” said the tree. Ravi took the branches and left.

Many years later, Ravi came back as an old man. “I am tired,” he said. “I want to go far away on a boat.”

“Cut my trunk and make a boat,” said the tree. Ravi did so.

At the end, only a small stump was left. Ravi, now very old, sat on it. “Thank you,” he said with tears.

The tree smiled. “I am happy,” it said. “I gave everything because I love you.”

Moral: Parents give us everything with love. Thank them.

title: The Bird with the Broken Wing
description: One windy morning, a little girl named Lily found a bird in her garden.
text:
One windy morning, a little girl named Lily found a bird in her garden. It was lying on the grass. It could not fly, and one of its wings was broken.

Lily picked it up carefully. “Don’t be afraid,” she said softly. “I will help you.”

She brought the bird home and put it in a small box with a soft cloth. Every day, she gave it water and little seeds. Her father helped her to tie the wing with a thin piece of cloth.

Weeks passed. The bird became stronger. Lily talked to it every day and sang songs. The bird listened and looked at her with its little eyes.

One sunny morning, the wing was healed. Lily took the bird outside. She felt sad, but she knew the right thing to do. “Now you are free,” she said.

She opened her hands. The bird flew up into the sky. It flew around her head one time and then went away over the trees.

Lily smiled with tears in her eyes. The next morning, she heard a song in her garden. The bird was sitting on the fence, singing for her.

Moral: Love means setting someone free.

title: The Fox and the Crow
description: A crow found a big piece of cheese.
text:
A crow found a big piece of cheese. She was very happy. She flew up to a high branch of a tree and sat there. She wanted to eat her cheese in peace.

A hungry fox walked past. He looked up and saw the cheese. “Mmm,” he thought. “I want that cheese. But how can I get it?”

He had an idea. He smiled and said, “Good morning, beautiful crow! You look so lovely today! Your feathers are shiny and black.”

The crow was surprised, but she felt proud.

“I heard that you have the sweetest voice in the forest,” said the fox. “Could you sing a song for me?”

The crow was very happy. “Of course!” she thought. She opened her mouth to sing, “Caw! Caw!”

The cheese fell down. The fox caught it quickly. “Thank you!” he said, and he ran away laughing.

The crow sat alone on the branch. “I was foolish,” she said sadly. “I listened to flattery.”

Moral: Be careful of people who say too many sweet words.

title: The Two Gifts
description: Anna and her husband Peter were very poor.
text:
Anna and her husband Peter were very poor. Christmas was coming, but they had no money for gifts.

Anna had long, beautiful hair. It was her greatest treasure. Peter had a silver watch from his grandfather. He loved it very much.

Anna wanted to buy a chain for Peter’s watch. So she went to a shop and sold her hair. With the money, she bought a beautiful chain.

At the same time, Peter wanted to buy combs for Anna’s long hair. So he sold his watch. With the money, he bought a set of lovely combs.

That evening, they met at home. Anna gave Peter the chain. “But I sold my watch,” said Peter, and he gave her the combs. “And I sold my hair,” said Anna.

They looked at each other. For a moment, they were silent. Then they began to laugh and hugged each other.

“Our gifts are useless now,” said Peter. “But we have each other. That is the best gift of all.”

Moral: Love is the greatest gift.

title: The Camel's Nose
description: One cold night, an Arab man was sleeping in his tent.
text:
One cold night, an Arab man was sleeping in his tent. His camel stood outside in the wind. The camel was cold and wanted to come in.

“Master,” said the camel, “it is very cold. Please, may I put just my nose inside the tent?”

The man was kind. “Okay,” he said. “Only your nose.”

The camel put his nose inside. A few minutes later, he said, “Master, my neck is cold too. May I put my neck in?”

“Okay,” said the man sleepily, “but only your neck.”

Then the camel asked for his front legs. And then for his shoulders. Little by little, he came into the tent.

At last, the camel said, “There is not much space here for both of us. You are small. You can go outside.”

And he pushed the man out of the tent into the cold night.

The man stood outside, shivering. “I was too kind in the beginning,” he said. “I should have said no at the first step.”

Moral: If you allow a small thing, bigger things will follow.

title: King Midas and the Golden Touch
description: Long ago, there was a king named Midas.
text:
Long ago, there was a king named Midas. He loved gold more than anything. He had a big palace full of gold, but he always wanted more.

One day, a kind god said, “Midas, I will give you one wish. What do you want?”

“I want everything I touch to turn into gold!” said Midas.

“Are you sure?” asked the god.

“Yes!”

“Then your wish is granted.”

Midas was very excited. He touched a chair, and it became gold. He touched a table, and it became gold. He laughed and laughed.

Soon, he felt hungry. He picked up a piece of bread. It turned into gold. He took a cup of water. The water turned into gold too! “What can I eat?” he cried.

Then his little daughter ran to him and hugged him. In a moment, she became a golden statue.

Midas fell to his knees and cried. “Please, take this power back!” he begged. “I don’t want gold. I want my daughter!”

The god heard him. He washed Midas’s hands in a river, and everything returned to normal.

Midas never wished for gold again.

Moral: Love and family are worth more than gold.

title: The Miller, His Son and the Donkey
description: A miller and his son were walking to the market with their donkey.
text:
A miller and his son were walking to the market with their donkey. They planned to sell it.

On the road, some women laughed. “Look at those fools! They have a donkey, but they walk!” The miller heard them. He put his son on the donkey.

Soon, they met some old men. “Shame on you!” said the men. “A young boy rides, and his old father walks!” So the miller changed places with his son.

Then they passed a group of travelers. “How selfish!” they said. “That man rides, and the little boy walks!” So the miller took his son up, and both rode the donkey.

A farmer saw them. “Poor donkey!” he said. “Two people are too heavy for him!”

The miller was tired and confused. He got down and tied the donkey’s legs. Then he and his son carried it on a pole.

When they crossed a bridge, the donkey kicked and fell into the river. It swam away and was gone.

The miller sat down sadly. “I tried to please everyone,” he said, “and now I have nothing.”

Moral: You cannot please everyone.

title: The Lost Wallet
description: Tom was a ten-year-old boy.
text:
Tom was a ten-year-old boy. One afternoon, he was walking home from school. He saw something brown on the road. It was a wallet.

He opened it. Inside, there was a lot of money and a card with a name and address: Mr. Brown, 12 Green Street.

Tom thought, “I could buy a new bicycle with this money. Nobody is looking at me.” He put the wallet in his bag and walked a few steps.

But then he stopped. He thought about the owner. “Maybe he needs this money for his family,” he thought. “I would be sad if I lost my money.”

Tom turned around. He walked to Green Street and knocked on the door of number 12.

An old man opened the door. “Is this your wallet?” asked Tom.

The old man’s eyes became wide. “Yes! I looked for it all day. It has my medicine money. Thank you so much!”

He gave Tom a little reward, but Tom said, “No, thank you. I only wanted to help.”

That night, Tom slept very well. He felt proud of himself.

Moral: Doing the right thing makes you feel good.

title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
description: A country mouse lived in a quiet field.
text:
A country mouse lived in a quiet field. His home was small, and his food was simple: seeds, grass, and a little cheese.

One day, his cousin, a town mouse, came to visit. “Your life is boring,” said the town mouse. “Come to my house in the city. You will eat the best food!”

The country mouse agreed. They walked to the big city. The town mouse’s house was beautiful. On the table, there was bread, cake, fruit, and cheese. “Eat!” said the town mouse.

The country mouse started to eat. Suddenly, the door opened with a loud noise. A big cat ran into the room! The mice ran and hid in a small hole. They were shaking.

After a few minutes, they came out and began to eat again. Then a dog barked, and they had to run again.

The country mouse stood up. “Thank you, cousin,” he said, “but I’m going home. Your food is delicious, but I am afraid all the time.”

He went back to his quiet field. He ate his simple seeds and felt safe and happy.

Moral: A simple, peaceful life is better than a rich life full of fear.

title: The Honest Woodcutter
description: A poor woodcutter worked near a river.
text:
A poor woodcutter worked near a river. Every day, he cut wood and sold it in the village. He had only one axe, and it was made of iron.

One morning, while he was cutting a tree, his axe slipped from his hand and fell into the deep river. “Oh no!” he cried. “How can I work now?” He sat on the ground and began to cry.

Suddenly, a kind spirit came out of the water. “Why are you crying?” it asked.

“I lost my axe,” said the woodcutter.

The spirit went into the river and came back with a golden axe. “Is this yours?”

“No,” said the woodcutter. “Mine was iron.”

The spirit brought a silver axe. “Is this yours?”

“No, that is not mine either.”

The third time, the spirit brought an iron axe. “Yes!” said the woodcutter happily. “This is my axe!”

The spirit smiled. “You are very honest. Take all three axes as a gift.”

The woodcutter thanked the spirit and went home. He was happy and rich.

Moral: Honesty is always rewarded.

title: The Milkmaid and Her Dream
description: A young girl named Rosa carried a bucket of milk on her head.
text:
A young girl named Rosa carried a bucket of milk on her head. She was walking to the market, and she was dreaming.

“I will sell this milk,” she thought, “and buy some eggs. The eggs will become chickens. I will sell the chickens and buy a beautiful new dress.”

She smiled. “Then I will go to the party. All the boys will look at me. But I will say no to them and turn my head like this.”

She turned her head proudly. The bucket fell off, and all the milk spilled on the road.

Rosa looked at the empty bucket. She wanted to cry. There was no milk, no eggs, no chickens, and no dress.

She went home slowly. Her mother asked, “What happened?” Rosa told her the whole story.

Her mother smiled kindly. “My dear,” she said, “dreams are nice, but watch the road today. First, do your work well. Then you can think about the future.”

Rosa nodded. The next day, she carried the milk carefully and sold it. With the money, she bought a small chicken. It was a little thing, but it was real.

Moral: Don’t count your chickens before they hatch.

title: The Farmer's Secret Treasure
description: An old farmer had three sons.
text:
An old farmer had three sons. They were lazy and never wanted to work in the vineyard. The farmer was worried because he was getting old and weak.

One day, he became very sick. He called his sons to his bed. “My sons,” he said quietly, “I have a secret. There is a treasure in our vineyard. I hid it many years ago, deep in the ground.”

“Where is it?” asked the sons.

“I cannot remember the exact place,” said the farmer. “You must dig and find it.” Then he closed his eyes and died.

After the funeral, the sons took their shovels. They dug the whole vineyard from morning to night. They dug every corner, but they found no gold or silver.

They were very sad. “Father lied to us,” said the oldest son.

But that autumn, something wonderful happened. Because the soil was so soft and deep, the grapes grew bigger and sweeter than ever before. The brothers sold them at the market and made a lot of money.

Now they understood. “This is the treasure our father meant,” said the youngest son. “Hard work is the real gold.”

From that day, the three brothers worked in the vineyard every year, and they were never poor again.

Moral: Hard work is the best treasure.

title: The Last Seat on the Bus
description: Sara was tired.
text:
Sara was tired. She had worked twelve hours, and her feet hurt. When the evening bus arrived, it was almost full. She found the last empty seat and sat down with a sigh.

At the next stop, an old woman climbed on. She was carrying two heavy shopping bags and looked exhausted. Nobody stood up. Everyone was looking at their phones.

Sara hesitated. She was so tired, and she thought, “Someone else will give her a seat.” But no one did. The old woman held on to a pole, shaking a little as the bus moved.

Sara stood up. “Please take my seat,” she said.

“Thank you, dear,” said the woman gratefully. She sat down, and Sara held her bags.

Ten minutes later, the woman said, “I have been shopping all day for my sick husband. I was feeling terrible and almost cried on the bus. You made my day better.”

Sara smiled. Strangely, she didn’t feel tired any more. She felt light and happy.

When the old woman got off, she touched Sara’s hand. “Remember,” she said, “small kindnesses give us more energy than a seat ever could.”

Sara walked the rest of the way home with a smile.

Moral: When we help others, we often help ourselves more.

title: The Violin in the Subway
description: One cold January morning, a man in jeans and a baseball cap stood in a busy subway station.
text:
One cold January morning, a man in jeans and a baseball cap stood in a busy subway station. He took a violin out of its case and began to play.

He played for forty-five minutes. Over a thousand people passed him on their way to work. Most of them didn’t even look at him. Only six people stopped for a moment, and he earned about thirty-two dollars.

Nobody knew that the violinist was one of the greatest musicians in the world. Two days earlier, he had played in a famous concert hall, where the tickets cost hundreds of dollars. The violin in his hands was worth millions.

A newspaper had organised the experiment to ask an important question: “Do we notice beauty when it appears in an unexpected place?”

Only one person recognised the music. She was a woman who had once heard him in a concert. She stood still, listening, with tears in her eyes.

When the experiment ended, a journalist asked her, “Why did you stop?”

“Because I couldn’t walk away,” she said. “How can the rest of us walk past something so wonderful?”

Moral: Beauty and wonder are everywhere, but we have to slow down to see them.

title: The Rain Maker
description: A terrible drought hit a farming village.
text:
A terrible drought hit a farming village. For six months, there was no rain. The crops died, and the animals were thin and weak.

The villagers invited a famous rain maker from the city. He arrived on a donkey, carrying a large bag. “I can bring rain,” he said. “But I need complete silence and one week of work.”

For seven days, he sat alone in a hut. Nobody was allowed to enter. He didn’t eat or drink much.

On the eighth day, dark clouds appeared in the sky, and a heavy rain began to fall. The villagers cheered and danced in the mud.

“How did you do it?” they asked. “What is your secret?”

The rain maker smiled. “I didn’t make the rain,” he said. “I don’t have magic powers. But when I arrive in a village, I wait until the weather changes. And when I come into a place that is full of worry, I first calm myself. Then I wait.”

“But the rain came after you!” said an old farmer.

“I came after the rain was already on its way,” said the man. “Sometimes, when we are patient and calm, things happen naturally.”

He took his bag and left the village before anyone could argue.

Moral: Patience and calm can solve many problems that fear and panic cannot.

title: The Parrot Who Told Secrets
description: Mr.
text:
Mr. Gray had a beautiful green parrot called Max. Max could repeat everything he heard, and visitors loved listening to him.

But Mr. Gray had a problem. He often gossiped about his neighbours at home, and Max repeated every word. One afternoon, while Mrs. Brown was visiting, the parrot said loudly, “Mrs. Brown is so boring! I hate her cooking!”

Mrs. Brown went red and left immediately. Mr. Gray was embarrassed, and he apologised for days.

The next week, the parrot told the postman that Mr. Gray was afraid of dogs. The week after that, he told a policeman that Mr. Gray never paid for parking.

Finally, Mr. Gray had enough. He sat down in front of the cage. “Max,” he said, “it’s my fault, not yours. You only repeat what you hear.”

From that day, Mr. Gray changed. He stopped gossiping and began to say only kind and polite things at home. Soon, his neighbours noticed the difference, and the visits became more pleasant.

One day, Max said clearly, “Mrs. Brown is a wonderful cook!”

Mrs. Brown, who was standing at the door, laughed and clapped her hands.

Moral: What we say will come back to us, so we should choose our words carefully.

title: The Bakery on the Corner
description: Every morning at four o’clock, Mr.
text:
Every morning at four o’clock, Mr. Carlo opened his little bakery. The smell of fresh bread filled the street, and many people stopped there before work.

A boy named Peter walked past the shop every day on his way to school. He never had money, so he only stood outside and smelled the bread.

One cold morning, Mr. Carlo noticed him. “Come in, young man,” he said. “I made too many rolls today. Please take one.”

Peter was surprised, but he took it. “Thank you,” he said. “I’ll pay you back someday.”

“No need,” said Mr. Carlo. “Just share something with somebody else when you can.”

Peter never forgot those words. Years later, he became a successful chef and opened his own restaurant. Every morning, before opening, he left a basket of fresh bread outside the door with a sign that said: “Take one. Share one.”

One day, an old man walked slowly past the restaurant. It was Mr. Carlo. His bakery had closed years ago, and he was living on a very small pension.

Peter ran outside. “Please come in,” he said with a big smile. “You’re my guest for the rest of your life.”

Moral: Small acts of generosity can grow into something wonderful.

title: The Letter That Never Arrived
description: Anna was seventeen when her best friend, Julia, moved to another country.
text:
Anna was seventeen when her best friend, Julia, moved to another country. They promised to write to each other every month.

Anna wrote her first letter the following week. She waited and waited for an answer, but nothing arrived. After three months, she stopped writing. “She has forgotten me,” she thought bitterly.

Twenty years passed. Anna became a nurse and married. One day, she was cleaning her mother’s attic when she found a small box. Inside there were twelve letters, all addressed to her, all in Julia’s handwriting.

Her hands began to shake. Her mother had hidden them, perhaps because she was afraid Anna would leave too. Anna read them one by one, crying and laughing at the same time. In each letter, Julia asked the same question: “Why don’t you write to me?”

That evening, Anna searched for Julia on the internet. After an hour, she found her. She wrote a short message: “I never forgot you. I only found your letters today.”

An answer came within minutes. “I never forgot you either. I have been waiting for twenty years.”

Three weeks later, they met at an airport and held each other without saying a word.

Moral: It’s never too late to repair a friendship.

title: The Blacksmith's Apprentice
description: Tom was proud when he became an apprentice to the village blacksmith.
text:
Tom was proud when he became an apprentice to the village blacksmith. But after a month, he was disappointed. Every day, the blacksmith only asked him to make nails, and Tom thought that was boring.

“When will I make something important?” he complained. “Swords? Armour? Tools for the king?”

The blacksmith said nothing. He just continued working.

One morning, a soldier came to the shop in a hurry. “My horse has lost a shoe,” he said. “I must reach the castle today. The king is in danger!”

The blacksmith looked at Tom. “Make a horseshoe,” he said. “Quickly.”

Tom’s hands moved by themselves. He heated the iron, shaped it and cooled it. He fixed the shoe to the horse’s foot in less than ten minutes.

The soldier thanked them and galloped away. Later, the village heard that he had arrived on time and saved the king’s life.

That evening, Tom sat next to his master. “Thank you,” he said quietly. “I understand now. Making all those nails taught me to work fast and well.”

The blacksmith nodded. “Small tasks prepare you for big moments,” he said. “You never know when your time will come.”

Moral: Every small task you do well is preparation for something great.

title: The Mountain Path
description: Two friends, Leo and Max, decided to climb a mountain.
text:
Two friends, Leo and Max, decided to climb a mountain. The path was long and steep, and by noon they were already exhausted.

“Let’s go back,” said Leo. “This is too hard. We’ll never reach the top.”

“We’ve come so far,” said Max. “Let’s rest and continue.”

They sat down and shared some water. A woman came down the path, carrying a heavy bag. She stopped to say hello.

“How far is the top?” asked Leo.

“About three hours,” said the woman. “But the view is worth it. I have just come from there.”

“Three hours!” said Leo. “That’s too much.”

The woman laughed. “Don’t think about the three hours. Think about the next hundred steps. Then the next hundred. That’s how I climb every day.”

The friends looked at each other. They stood up and started walking, counting their steps in hundreds. It felt easier, and time seemed to move faster.

At sunset, they reached the summit. The whole valley lay below them, golden in the evening light. They couldn’t speak for a long time.

“Imagine if we had gone back,” said Max quietly.

Moral: Big challenges become possible when you divide them into small parts.

title: The Stranger at the Door
description: It was a stormy night, and the Millers were having dinner when somebody knocked on the door.
text:
It was a stormy night, and the Millers were having dinner when somebody knocked on the door. Mrs. Miller opened it and saw a tired old man in a wet coat.

“I’m sorry to disturb you,” he said. “My car has broken down, and there are no hotels nearby. Could I stay by your fire until the morning?”

Mr. Miller hesitated. They didn’t know the man. But he looked harmless, and the weather was terrible. “Come in,” he said finally.

They gave him hot soup and a warm blanket. The old man was very polite. He told them stories about his travels and made their children laugh. By midnight, they were all friends.

In the morning, the storm had passed. The man thanked them and walked out to the road. A few minutes later, a car arrived. Two men in suits jumped out and hurried to him. “Sir, we have been looking for you all night!”

Mrs. Miller was surprised. “Who is he?” she whispered to her husband.

A week later, they received a letter. It was from the old man, who was the owner of a large company. Inside was a cheque and a short note: “Thank you for opening your door when you did not need to.”

Moral: Kindness to strangers is never a waste.

title: The Village Bridge
description: A wide, fast river separated two villages.
text:
A wide, fast river separated two villages. For many years, the people on both sides wanted a bridge, but they never agreed about who should build it or pay for it.

One year, a heavy storm destroyed the old wooden boat that people used to cross the water. After that, the villagers couldn’t visit each other at all. Their relatives were on the other side, and the children couldn’t go to school.

Finally, an old man named Yusuf stood up in the meeting. “We have argued for thirty years,” he said. “And what have we got? Nothing. I’m going to start building the bridge tomorrow morning. Anyone who wants to help can join me.”

The next day, he arrived at the river with a hammer and some wood. At first, he was alone. By lunchtime, three more people had come. By the end of the week, there were fifty workers from both villages.

They worked side by side for two months. At the end, there was a strong bridge across the river. The people from both sides met in the middle, shook hands and cried.

“Why didn’t we do this before?” asked one man.

“Because nobody wanted to be the first,” said Yusuf with a smile.

Moral: Someone has to take the first step, and it can be you.

title: The Painter and the Critic
description: A young painter spent six months working on a portrait.
text:
A young painter spent six months working on a portrait. When it was finished, he put it in the town square and wrote a sign next to it: “Please mark every mistake with a red cross.”

By the evening, the painting was covered in red crosses. The painter felt terrible and went home in tears.

His teacher visited him that night. “Why are you crying?” he asked.

“Everybody hated my painting,” said the young man. “Look how many mistakes they found!”

The teacher thought for a moment. “Tomorrow, make another copy of the painting,” he said. “This time, write a different sign: ‘Please mark the parts you like with a green circle.’”

The painter did as he was told. By the end of the next day, the second painting was covered in green circles. Many people had marked exactly the same parts that others had crossed out the day before.

The painter was confused. “I don’t understand,” he said.

“You can’t please everyone,” said the teacher. “Every person sees something different. Listen to the advice you can learn from, but don’t let it destroy your confidence.”

The painter smiled for the first time in two days.

Moral: Opinions are different, so don’t let criticism stop you.

title: The Fisherman's Net
description: An old fisherman lived on the coast.
text:
An old fisherman lived on the coast. Every day, he threw his net into the sea, and every day it came back almost empty. He was tired and poor, and he was losing hope.

One evening, he sat on the beach and spoke to himself. “Maybe I should stop. The sea doesn’t want to give me fish anymore.”

A young boy was sitting nearby and heard him. “Excuse me, sir,” he said. “Why do you only fish near the rocks?”

“Because I have always fished here,” said the old man. “My father did it, and his father too.”

“But the other fishermen go to the north bay,” said the boy. “My uncle caught twenty fish there yesterday.”

The old man was silent. He had never thought about that. For forty years, he had used the same place and the same method, and he had expected different results.

The next morning, he took his boat to the north bay. It was frightening at first because the water was deep and unfamiliar. But when he pulled up his net, it was heavy and full of silver fish.

He laughed out loud. “Forty years,” he said to the sea. “Why did I wait so long?”

Moral: If you want different results, try something different.

title: The King's Messenger
description: A king once chose a young man to carry an important letter to a faraway city.
text:
A king once chose a young man to carry an important letter to a faraway city. “Ride quickly,” said the king. “The letter must arrive before the end of the week.”

The messenger left at sunrise. On the road, he saw many things that tried to stop him. A beautiful garden invited him to rest. A friendly farmer offered him a delicious meal. A group of travellers asked him to join their party.

“I’m sorry,” said the messenger each time. “I have a duty to do.”

On the fourth day, he met an old man by the road. The old man was lying on the ground, and he looked very ill. “Please help me,” he said weakly. “I need a doctor.”

The messenger stopped. He knew he would be late if he helped. But he couldn’t leave a sick man alone. He carried him to a nearby village and found a doctor.

He arrived at the city a day late. He knelt in front of the king’s friend and gave him the letter. “I’m sorry I’m late,” he said.

The man read it and smiled. “This letter says: ‘Choose the messenger who stops to help a stranger. He is the one I need.’”

Moral: Kindness is more important than speed.

title: The Girl Who Fixed Clocks
description: Nora lived with her grandfather above a small clock shop.
text:
Nora lived with her grandfather above a small clock shop. She loved watching him repair old watches, and by the age of twelve, she could fix most of them herself.

One day, a rich man came into the shop with a huge golden clock. “It stopped working,” he said. “Three other shops couldn’t repair it. Can you do it?”

Nora’s grandfather was ill in bed, so she said, “I’ll try.”

She worked for three days. She opened the clock, cleaned every tiny wheel and checked every spring. On the third day, she found the problem. It was a very small piece of dust, almost invisible, stuck between two wheels.

She carefully removed it, and the clock began to tick.

The rich man was very happy. “How much do I owe you?” he asked.

“Fifty dollars,” said Nora.

“Fifty dollars for a speck of dust?” he said angrily.

“No,” she said. “Ten dollars for removing the dust. Forty dollars for knowing where it was.”

The man stared at her for a moment. Then he laughed and paid her double.

Moral: Knowledge and experience are worth more than the work itself.

title: The Silent Bell
description: In the middle of a small town, there was a tall tower with a big bell.
text:
In the middle of a small town, there was a tall tower with a big bell. People said the bell was magic. According to the old story, it would ring by itself if somebody did something truly good.

For many years, the bell stayed silent. People tried many things. The mayor built a new school, but the bell didn’t ring. A rich merchant gave a lot of money to the church, but the bell was still silent.

One cold winter night, an old woman was walking home. She saw a little dog shivering in the snow. She had very little money, and her coat was thin, but she took the dog home, gave it her dinner and let it sleep by the fire.

She didn’t tell anybody about it. In the morning, she opened the door and heard a deep, beautiful sound across the town. Everybody stopped in the street and looked up.

The bell was ringing.

People ran to the tower. They were confused. “Who did something so good?” they asked.

Nobody knew. The old woman sat quietly in her kitchen, stroking the dog. She never learned that the bell had rung for her.

Moral: The best kind deeds are the ones we do without wanting any reward.

title: Two Brothers and the Well
description: Two brothers lived in a dry village.
text:
Two brothers lived in a dry village. There was only one well, and it was almost empty. Every day, the villagers argued about the water.

One of the brothers, Daud, said, “We should dig a new well. It will take months, but it will help everybody.”

The other brother, Samir, laughed. “Why should we work for the whole village? Let’s keep what we have. Let’s hide the water in our house.”

“That’s selfish,” said Daud. “I’m going to dig.” He took a shovel and walked out of the house.

Every morning, Daud dug in the hot sun. Many people laughed at him. “You’re wasting your time,” they said. “There’s no water down there.”

Samir, meanwhile, took water from the old well at night. But soon the well was completely dry, and he had nothing.

After three months, Daud’s shovel hit something wet. A cool stream of water came out of the ground. He shouted with joy, and the whole village ran to see it.

“Come and drink,” he said to everybody. Then he looked at Samir, who was standing at the back. “You too, brother.”

Samir felt ashamed, but he drank. After that day, he helped Daud look after the well.

Moral: When we work for everyone, everyone benefits, including us.

title: The Old Tailor's Last Lesson
description: Mr.
text:
Mr. Hassan had been a tailor for fifty years. His shop was small and old, but the best families in the city came to him for their suits.

When he became too old to work, his apprentice, Omar, took over the shop. On the last day, Mr. Hassan said, “I have one more lesson for you.”

He gave Omar a beautiful suit. “Look at it carefully,” he said. “Tell me what you see.”

Omar studied the suit. “The cloth is excellent. The stitches are perfect. The buttons are very strong.”

“Now turn it inside out,” said Mr. Hassan.

Omar did that and was surprised. The inside was as perfect as the outside. Every seam was neat and every thread was in the right place.

“Nobody will ever see the inside of this suit,” said Omar. “Why did you spend so much time on it?”

“I will see it,” said the old man. “And you will, too. A good tailor doesn’t work for the customer’s eyes. He works for his own conscience.”

Omar remembered those words for the rest of his life. His shop became famous, but his greatest pride was always in the parts that nobody could see.

Moral: Do your best even when nobody is watching.

title: The Clever Judge
description: A long time ago, two women came to a judge.
text:
A long time ago, two women came to a judge. Both of them were holding a baby boy, and both of them said, “This is my son!”

The judge looked at them carefully. There were no witnesses, and nobody could prove anything. The women were crying and shouting, and the baby was frightened.

“Be quiet, please,” said the judge. “I have a solution.” He called his servant. “Bring me a sword.”

The women stopped shouting. The servant returned with the sword.

“Cut the baby in two,” said the judge. “Each woman will take one half. That’s fair.”

The first woman said nothing. She just looked at the floor. But the second woman cried out, “No, please! Don’t hurt him! Give the baby to her. I would rather lose him than see him die!”

The judge smiled and lifted his hand. “Stop,” he said. He turned to the second woman. “Take your son. Only a real mother would give up her child to save his life.”

The first woman had lied because she wanted a baby for herself. The guards took her away.

The judge returned the baby to his mother, and she thanked him again and again.

Moral: True love thinks of the other person first.

title: The Tea Master's Gift
description: In a quiet town lived a famous tea master.
text:
In a quiet town lived a famous tea master. People travelled from far away to learn from him, and many of them hoped to become rich teachers one day.

A young woman named Mei arrived at his house early one morning. “I want to learn everything about tea,” she said. “How long will it take?”

“Ten years,” said the master.

“Ten years? That’s too long! What if I work twice as hard?”

“Then it will take twenty years,” he said calmly.

Mei was surprised and a little angry, but she stayed. For the first year, the master gave her only one job: she washed the cups. She washed them again and again, and she felt bored and frustrated.

One day, she finally asked, “When will I learn the real secrets?”

The master smiled. “Bring me a cup of tea.”

Mei made the tea quickly and gave it to him. He tasted it and shook his head. “You were thinking about tomorrow. I can taste it.”

Mei understood. She made another cup, slowly, thinking only about the water, the leaves and her hands.

The master tasted it again and closed his eyes. “Now,” he said quietly, “you have learned the first secret.”

Moral: Be present in what you are doing right now, because rushing spoils everything.

title: The Golden Bowl
description: A young man called Kenji owned a beautiful blue bowl.
text:
A young man called Kenji owned a beautiful blue bowl. His grandmother had given it to him before she died, and he used it every day.

One morning, he dropped it. The bowl broke into five pieces. Kenji sat on the floor and felt terrible. “It’s ruined,” he said. “It has lost all its value.”

He put the pieces in a box and almost threw them away. But a neighbour, an old craftsman, saw him in the street. “What’s in the box?” he asked.

“A broken bowl,” said Kenji sadly.

“Let me see it,” said the old man. “Maybe I can help.”

A week later, the craftsman returned the bowl. Kenji could not believe his eyes. The pieces were joined together with thin lines of shining gold. The bowl looked different, but it was more beautiful than before.

“I don’t understand,” said Kenji. “Why did you use gold?”

“In my country, we don’t hide broken things,” the craftsman answered. “We show their history. Every crack tells a story, and the story makes the object special.”

Kenji looked at the golden lines. He thought about his own mistakes and the difficult times in his life. For the first time, he did not feel ashamed.

He put the bowl on the table in the middle of his room, where everybody could see it.

Moral: Our scars and mistakes can make us more beautiful, not less.

title: The Man Who Wanted to Change the World
description: When he was young, a man wrote in his diary, “I want to change the world.” He worked hard for years, but the world did not change.
text:
When he was young, a man wrote in his diary, “I want to change the world.” He worked hard for years, but the world did not change.

At middle age, he wrote, “I have failed. I will change my country instead.” He gave speeches and organised meetings, but his country stayed the same.

When he turned sixty, he said, “I will change my town.” Again, nothing much happened. People listened politely and then went home.

At seventy, he sat alone in a small room, tired and sad. “Maybe I should have started with my own family,” he thought. He called his children and grandchildren and apologised for the many years he had spent away from them. He listened to their problems and began to help them. For the first time, he felt that he was doing something real.

Slowly, his family changed. His children became kinder to each other, and his grandchildren learned to be generous. Neighbours noticed it and asked how it was possible.

When he was eighty, a journalist visited his house. “If I could start again,” the old man told her, “I would begin with myself. Then I would change my family. With their help, I might have changed my town. And who knows? Maybe even the world.”

Moral: Change begins at home, with ourselves.

title: The Coffee, the Carrot and the Egg
description: A young woman complained to her mother that life was too hard.
text:
A young woman complained to her mother that life was too hard. “As soon as I solve one problem, another one appears,” she said. “I’m tired of struggling.”

Her mother took her into the kitchen and filled three pots with water. She put a carrot in the first pot, an egg in the second and some coffee beans in the third. She boiled them all for twenty minutes.

Then she took out the carrot and the egg and poured the coffee into a cup. “What do you see?” she asked.

“A soft carrot, a hard egg, and a cup of coffee,” said the daughter.

“Look carefully,” said the mother. “The carrot was strong, but boiling water made it weak and soft. The egg was fragile with a liquid inside, but the heat made it hard. The coffee beans were different. They changed the water itself and made it fragrant.”

The daughter picked up the cup and smiled slowly. “Which one am I?”

“That’s the question,” said her mother. “When difficulties come, do you become weak? Do you become hard and bitter? Or do you change your surroundings and turn the situation into something better?”

The young woman drank the coffee in silence. When she left the kitchen, she felt that her problems had become smaller.

Moral: You can’t choose your difficulties, but you can choose how to respond to them.

title: The Eagle Who Thought He Was a Chicken
description: A farmer found an eagle’s egg on a mountain and took it home.
text:
A farmer found an eagle’s egg on a mountain and took it home. He put it under a hen with her own eggs. In a few weeks, a baby eagle hatched alongside the chicks.

The young eagle grew up with the chickens. He ate the same food, scratched the ground and made the same noises. He never flew higher than a few metres, because that was what the chickens did.

Years later, a naturalist visited the farm. He saw the huge bird walking among the hens and cried out, “That’s an eagle! Why is he living like a chicken?”

“I raised him as a chicken,” said the farmer. “He believes that he is one.”

“But he has the heart of an eagle,” said the naturalist. He picked up the bird and lifted him high into the air. “You belong to the sky!” he shouted.

The eagle looked at the ground in fear and jumped back down to the chickens. The naturalist tried again and again, but each time the eagle returned to the yard.

Finally, the man took the bird to the top of a mountain at sunrise. The eagle felt the wind in his feathers, saw the golden sun in front of him and opened his wings. For the first time, he flew.

Moral: You may be capable of much more than the people around you believe.

title: The Quiet Student
description: In a large classroom, there was a boy named Adam who never spoke.
text:
In a large classroom, there was a boy named Adam who never spoke. He sat in the last row and looked at his desk. Some students laughed at him, and others simply forgot that he existed.

His teacher, Mrs. Lopez, noticed him. She didn’t force him to speak. Instead, she began to write small comments on his homework: “This is a clever idea.” “I like the way you think.” “I’d love to hear more about this.”

At first, Adam didn’t react. But after a few weeks, he started to write longer answers. After a few months, he began to raise his hand, only once or twice, and very quietly.

One day, the class was discussing a difficult poem. Nobody understood it. Mrs. Lopez looked at Adam, and he spoke clearly for the first time. His interpretation was so thoughtful that the whole room fell silent.

At the end of the school year, Adam wrote a letter to his teacher. “Thank you for seeing me,” he wrote. “I thought that nobody would care what I think. You showed me that my voice mattered.”

Mrs. Lopez kept the letter in her desk for the rest of her career. When she felt tired or discouraged, she took it out and read it again.

Moral: Sometimes a small word of encouragement can open a person’s whole future.

title: The Block of Marble
description: A sculptor was working in his studio when a young visitor asked him, “How do you create such beautiful statues?
text:
A sculptor was working in his studio when a young visitor asked him, “How do you create such beautiful statues? It must be very difficult.”

The sculptor laughed and pointed to a large block of marble in the corner. “That is my next work,” he said. “Come back in three months.”

When the visitor returned, a magnificent horse stood in the studio. Its muscles looked alive, and its eyes seemed to shine. The young man could hardly speak.

“How did you do it?” he whispered.

“It was simple,” said the sculptor. “I looked at the marble, and I saw a horse inside it. Then I removed everything that wasn’t a horse.”

The visitor smiled, thinking that the sculptor was joking, but the old man was serious. “Most people think that art is about adding,” he said. “In my experience, it’s mostly about taking away. The statue was always there. I only had to be patient and brave enough to remove the stone around it.”

The young man went home and thought about his own life. He had so many habits and worries that hid his true self. That night, he began to ask himself which parts of his life were not really him, and he decided to let them go.

Moral: Often, becoming your best self means removing what doesn’t belong to you.

title: The Shortcut
description: A traveller was walking to a distant city.
text:
A traveller was walking to a distant city. At a crossroads, he met an old man selling water. “Which road is the fastest?” the traveller asked.

“There are two,” said the old man. “The main road is long, with many curves, and it takes about five days. The shortcut through the forest takes only two days, but I have never met anyone who arrived safely.”

“Surely you’re exaggerating,” said the traveller, and he chose the shortcut. He thought the old man was only trying to sell him more water.

At first, everything went well. The path was straight and the weather was fine. By the second afternoon, however, he realised that he was lost. The trees were thick, the path had vanished, and he had run out of food. He wandered for four more days, hungry and frightened.

At last, a hunter found him and led him out of the forest. The traveller had lost his bag, his shoes and a lot of time. In total, the journey took him nine days.

When he finally reached the city, he told his story to a merchant. The merchant smiled sadly. “The main road would have been quicker,” he said. “People always think shortcuts save time. Most of the time, they only teach you a lesson.”

Moral: The easiest path is not always the fastest one.

title: The Gardener's Apprentice
description: A young man called Paulo became an apprentice to an old gardener.
text:
A young man called Paulo became an apprentice to an old gardener. On the first day, the gardener gave him a task. “Pull out all the weeds in this flower bed,” he said.

Paulo worked for hours. By the evening, the flower bed looked perfect. He called the old man proudly, but the gardener only shook his head. “Come back in two weeks.”

Two weeks later, Paulo returned and saw that the weeds had grown back, thicker than before. He was disappointed. “Why did I work so hard if they just came back?” he asked.

“Because you only cut the leaves,” said the gardener. “You didn’t pull out the roots. If you leave the roots, the weeds will always return.”

The next time, Paulo dug deep into the soil and removed every root. It took three times as long, and his hands were sore. But the flower bed stayed clean for months.

“This is true for more than gardens,” said the old man. “When you have a bad habit, it’s easy to remove it for a few days. But if you don’t deal with the reason behind it, it will come back.”

Paulo thought about his own habit of staying up late and being tired at work. That night, he did not just go to bed early. He asked himself why he stayed up, and he changed the cause, not just the symptom.

Moral: To solve a problem for good, deal with its root, not only its surface.

title: The Lighthouse Keeper
description: On a rocky island far from the mainland, there lived an old man whose job was to keep a lighthouse.
text:
On a rocky island far from the mainland, there lived an old man whose job was to keep a lighthouse. Every evening, he climbed two hundred steps to light the great lamp. Every morning, he climbed up again to clean it.

A young sailor who had been rescued from a storm stayed with him for a few days. He watched the old man’s routine and finally asked, “Don’t you ever get bored? You do the same thing every day, and sometimes months pass without a single ship.”

The old man smiled. “Do you know how many ships have passed this island in thirty years?”

“Thousands, I guess.”

“Thousands,” said the keeper. “And I have never met most of the people on board. But every night, I know that someone out there is looking for my light. If I forget it, even once, a ship might hit the rocks.”

The sailor looked out at the dark sea. “I never thought about it like that. I only remember being thankful for a light when I was lost.”

“That’s the secret of my job,” said the old man. “I don’t see the results, but I know they exist. Every night, I’m saving lives I will never know.”

When the sailor left, he promised to come back. Years later, he returned as a captain, and he brought a new lamp as a gift.

Moral: Meaningful work doesn’t always bring praise, but it still changes lives.

title: The Job Interview
description: Fifty candidates were waiting in a large hall for a job interview at a successful company.
text:
Fifty candidates were waiting in a large hall for a job interview at a successful company. They were all dressed in their best suits, and each of them had an impressive CV.

When the manager arrived, he walked past all of them without a word. On the floor near the entrance, there was a piece of paper. Many people had stepped over it. Some had even kicked it. But a young woman named Hannah picked it up, saw that it was just rubbish and put it into a bin.

The manager noticed, but he said nothing.

The interviews lasted the whole day. One by one, the candidates answered the questions about their experience and skills. Hannah wasn’t the most qualified person in the room, and she felt nervous. She was sure that she wouldn’t get the job.

At the end of the day, the manager called everybody back into the hall. “Thank you all for coming,” he said. “We have chosen the person who will work with us. It’s Hannah.”

Several candidates complained. “She had less experience than I did!” one man protested.

“That’s true,” said the manager. “But the paper on the floor was part of the interview. I can teach skills. I can’t teach someone to care.”

Moral: Character shows in the small things we do when we think no one is checking.

title: The Old Dog and the Puppy
description: An old dog named Rex lived on a farm.
text:
An old dog named Rex lived on a farm. He was slow and grey, and he slept most of the day. Then the farmer brought home a lively puppy named Buddy, who ran around the yard barking at everything.

“Why do you sleep so much?” asked Buddy. “You’re so boring! Come and play with me!”

“I’m tired, young one,” said Rex. “I’ve worked hard for ten years.”

Buddy ignored him and continued running in circles. One day, he found a small hole in the fence and squeezed through it. Soon he was in the forest, excited by the strange smells and sounds.

Then he saw something move in the bushes. It was a fox, and it was looking straight at him. Buddy froze. He wanted to run, but his legs wouldn’t move.

Suddenly, a deep bark shook the air. Rex had followed him. The old dog stepped in front of the puppy and showed his teeth. His voice was low and fierce. The fox hesitated, then turned and disappeared into the trees.

On the way home, Buddy walked quietly beside the old dog. “I’m sorry,” he said. “I didn’t understand.”

“You were curious,” said Rex. “That’s good. But wisdom comes from experience, not from speed.”

From then on, Buddy listened to Rex and learned everything the old dog could teach him.

Moral: Respect the experience of older people, because they have seen what you haven’t.

title: The Two Merchants
description: In a busy market town, two merchants sold the same kind of cloth.
text:
In a busy market town, two merchants sold the same kind of cloth. The first, Mr. Brown, always set low prices. He also used a trick: he measured the cloth with a ruler that was slightly too short, so customers received a little less than they paid for.

The second merchant, Mr. White, charged a bit more. But he measured honestly and sometimes added a small extra piece for free.

At first, Mr. Brown was winning. His shop was crowded because of his low prices, and Mr. White had few customers. “You’re a fool,” Mr. Brown told his rival. “Honesty doesn’t pay.”

Mr. White only shrugged. “We’ll see.”

Gradually, customers began to notice. A woman measured her cloth at home and found that it was too short. She told her neighbours, and the rumour spread quickly through the town. People started to avoid Mr. Brown’s shop.

Meanwhile, Mr. White’s regular customers told their friends how fair he was. Little by little, his shop became the most popular in the market. Even the rich families of the region bought their cloth from him.

After a year, Mr. Brown had to close his shop. Before he left town, he visited Mr. White. “You were right,” he said bitterly. “I lost everything for a few extra coins.”

Moral: A good reputation is worth more than a quick profit.

title: The Chess Master
description: A famous chess master was walking in a park when he noticed a young boy playing against his grandfather.
text:
A famous chess master was walking in a park when he noticed a young boy playing against his grandfather. The boy played with great enthusiasm but made one mistake after another.

The master stopped and watched for a while. When the game ended, the boy looked at him sadly. “I lost again,” he said. “I’m never going to be good at this.”

“May I play against you?” asked the master.

The boy was astonished. He sat down and played the best game of his life, but of course he lost in only fifteen moves.

“Don’t be sad,” said the master. “You played well. Do you know the difference between a beginner and an expert? It’s not talent. It’s the number of games they have lost.”

The boy raised his eyebrows. “Lost?”

“I have lost thousands of games,” said the master. “Every time, I asked myself one question: what can I learn? Losing was my best teacher. Winning only told me what I already knew.”

The boy sat up straight and set up the pieces again. “Can we play once more?”

“As many times as you like,” said the master with a smile.

They played until the sun went down. Twelve years later, the boy won a national championship. In his speech, he thanked a stranger in a park who had taught him to love losing.

Moral: Failure is not the opposite of success, but a necessary part of it.

title: The Librarian's Rule
text:
Miss Harper had been the town librarian for forty years, and she had only one rule: “Return every book exactly as you found it.”

Many people thought the rule was strange. Some borrowers tried to argue with her. “Why does it matter? It’s just a book,” they said.

One day, a teenage boy named Felix borrowed a rare old book about astronomy. He read it in the park, and when he got up to leave, he accidentally left a coffee stain on the cover. He was afraid to return it. For three weeks, he kept the book hidden in his room.

Finally, he went back to the library with his head down. “Miss Harper, I damaged the book,” he said, and he explained everything.

To his surprise, she wasn’t angry. “Do you know why I have my rule?” she asked. “It isn’t about the book. It’s about respect. When you borrow something, you carry the trust of a person you may never meet. The next reader deserves to find what you found.”

She repaired the cover herself. Then she gave Felix a job in the library, shelving books on Saturdays.

Felix worked there for six years. Today, he is the head of a university library, and a small sign hangs behind his desk: “Return every book exactly as you found it.”

Moral: Respect what is lent to you, because someone else will need it after you.

title: The Broken Window
description: Daniel and his friends were playing football in the street when his shot went wrong.
text:
Daniel and his friends were playing football in the street when his shot went wrong. The ball flew through the window of Mrs. Kelly’s house, and the glass smashed loudly.

His friends ran away at once. Daniel hesitated. He could hear his own heart beating. He could run home and pretend that nothing had happened. Nobody had seen him.

But he looked at the broken glass and imagined the old woman sitting alone in the cold. He knew she couldn’t afford to fix the window easily. He took a deep breath, walked up to the door and knocked.

“Mrs. Kelly,” he said, with a shaking voice, “I broke your window. I’m very sorry. I’d like to pay for it, but I don’t have much money. Can I work for you instead?”

The old woman looked at him for a long moment. “Most boys would have run away,” she said. “Come in.”

For the next month, Daniel mowed her lawn, did her shopping and cleaned her garden every weekend. In the end, they became friends. She baked him cakes and told him stories about her youth.

Years later, Daniel often said that it was the best mistake he ever made. “Running away would have been easy,” he said. “But I would never have met the person who taught me what responsibility means.”

Moral: Admitting your mistakes takes courage, and it can turn a bad moment into a good one.

title: The Window and the Mirror
text:
A rich man visited a wise rabbi and asked him, “Why are some people so generous while others are so selfish?”

The rabbi took him to the window. “What do you see?” he asked.

“I see people in the street,” said the rich man. “A mother with a child, some workers, a few beggars.”

Then the rabbi led him to a mirror. “And now?”

“I see myself,” the man answered.

“Both the window and the mirror are made of glass,” said the rabbi. “The only difference is a thin layer of silver. When you add silver, you can no longer see other people. You only see yourself.”

The rich man frowned. He was thinking about his large house, his bank accounts and the beggars he usually avoided.

“When we are surrounded by wealth,” continued the rabbi, “it’s easy to look only at ourselves. Silver can make us blind to the needs of others. But a person who looks through the clear glass sees the world as it really is, and he feels responsible for it.”

The rich man left the room without saying much. The next morning, he opened the door of his house and stopped to talk to a beggar for the first time in many years. It was a small beginning, but it changed him.

Moral: Don’t let wealth turn your window into a mirror.

title: The Elephant and the Rope
description: A tourist visited a village in India and noticed something strange.
text:
A tourist visited a village in India and noticed something strange. Next to a temple stood a huge elephant. It was tied to a post with only a thin rope. The tourist was amazed. The elephant could easily break the rope and walk away, yet it stood quietly.

He asked the owner, “Why doesn’t he escape? He is so strong!”

The owner smiled. “When he was a baby, we tied him to this same post with the same kind of rope. At that time, it was strong enough to hold him. He pulled and pulled, but he couldn’t break free. After many attempts, he accepted that the rope was stronger than he was.”

“And now?”

“Now he is a grown elephant, but he still believes that he can’t escape. He never tries. In his mind, the rope is as strong as it was twenty years ago.”

The tourist was silent. He remembered a business idea he had never tried because a friend had once told him that it would fail. He thought about all the things he had been afraid to attempt because of a failure long ago.

That evening, he sat in his hotel room and wrote a list of everything that he had given up too early. Then, one by one, he decided to try again.

Moral: Many of the limits in our lives exist only in our minds.

title: The Emperor's New Clothes
description: Many years ago, an emperor loved beautiful clothes more than anything else.
text:
Many years ago, an emperor loved beautiful clothes more than anything else. He spent all his money on them and changed his outfit every hour.

One day, two men arrived in the city. They claimed to be weavers who could make a magical cloth. “This fabric has a special quality,” they said. “It is invisible to anyone who is stupid or unfit for his job.”

The emperor was delighted. “With this cloth, I can discover who is foolish in my kingdom!” He paid the men a large amount of gold, and they began to work at empty looms.

After a few days, the emperor sent his minister to check the progress. The minister saw nothing, but he was afraid to say so. “It’s wonderful,” he said. “The colours are magnificent!”

At last the emperor himself came. He saw nothing, either, but he too was afraid. “Beautiful!” he said. The weavers pretended to dress him, and the emperor walked through the city in his invisible clothes.

The crowd cheered, because nobody wanted to look stupid. Then a small child said loudly, “But he isn’t wearing anything!”

The crowd began to whisper, and soon everybody was laughing. The emperor knew the child was right, but he continued the parade with his head held high.

The two weavers had already disappeared with the gold.

Moral: Don’t be afraid to tell the truth, even when everybody else is pretending.

title: The Carpenter's Last House
description: An old carpenter was ready to retire.
text:
An old carpenter was ready to retire. He told his boss that he wanted to spend more time with his wife and grandchildren. The boss was sorry to lose such a skilled worker and asked him to build one last house as a personal favour.

The carpenter agreed, but his heart wasn’t in the work. He used cheap wood, ignored small mistakes, and finished the job quickly. It was the worst work of his whole career.

When the house was ready, the boss came to inspect it. He walked through the rooms and then handed the carpenter a key. “This is your house,” he said. “It’s my gift to you for all your years of faithful service.”

The carpenter was shocked. He stared at the key in his hand and felt a heavy weight in his chest. If he had known he was building his own home, he would have done everything differently. He would have chosen the best materials and checked every window and every door. Now he would have to live in a house full of cracks and crooked walls, and he knew that he had built it himself.

Years later, he often sat on the porch and looked at the uneven floors. His grandchildren didn’t notice any problems, but he did. Every day he saw his own carelessness.

He used to say to young workers, “Treat every job as if it were your own house.”

Moral: Our life is a house we build every day, so we should build it with care.

title: The Salt and the Lake
description: A young man came to an old teacher and complained about his life.
text:
A young man came to an old teacher and complained about his life. “Everything is bitter,” he said. “My job is hard, my friends disappoint me, and I feel unhappy all the time.”

The teacher listened silently. Then he handed the young man a glass of water and a spoonful of salt. “Put the salt in the water and drink it,” he said.

The young man did so and immediately made a face. “It’s disgusting!”

The teacher smiled and led him to a small lake behind the house. “Now put the same amount of salt in the lake,” he said. The young man poured the salt into the water and stirred it with a stick.

“Now drink some of the lake water.”

The young man knelt down and drank from his hands. “It’s fresh,” he said, surprised. “I can’t taste the salt at all.”
