“The salt was exactly the same,” said the teacher. “The pain in life is also the same for everybody. Troubles will always come. But how bitter they taste depends on the size of the container that holds them.”

The young man thought about this.

“When you feel unhappy, stop being a glass,” the teacher continued. “Become a lake. Widen your view. Think about your family, your health, and the beauty around you. Then the bitterness will become only a small part of a much bigger life.”

The young man went home with a lighter heart. From that day, whenever he felt miserable, he remembered the lake.

Moral: You cannot avoid pain, but you can make your mind big enough to hold it.

title: The Glass of Water
description: A psychology professor stood in front of her class holding a glass of water.
text:
A psychology professor stood in front of her class holding a glass of water. The students expected the usual question: “Is it half full or half empty?” Instead, she asked, “How heavy do you think this glass is?”

The students gave different answers, from two hundred to five hundred grams.

“The actual weight doesn’t matter,” she said. “What matters is how long I hold it. If I hold it for a minute, it’s no problem. If I hold it for an hour, my arm will start to ache. If I hold it for a whole day, my arm will go numb, and I won’t be able to move it. The glass hasn’t changed, but the longer I carry it, the heavier it feels.”

She put the glass down on the desk.

“Your worries are like this glass,” she continued. “If you think about them for a short time, they cause you no harm. If you think about them all day, they begin to hurt. If you carry them for weeks, you’ll feel paralysed, unable to do anything else.”

A student at the back raised his hand. “So should we just ignore our problems?”

“No,” she said. “You should face them, think about solutions, and then put them down. Many people carry their troubles to bed every night and wake up exhausted. Learn to put the glass down before you go to sleep. Tomorrow, you can pick it up again if you need to, but you’ll be stronger.”

The students left the room quietly. Many of them were thinking about what they had been carrying for too long.

Moral: Deal with your worries, then put them down, because carrying them too long makes them heavier.

title: The Seed in the Desert
description: Long ago, a traveller crossing a vast desert noticed a small green plant growing between two enormous rocks.
text:
Long ago, a traveller crossing a vast desert noticed a small green plant growing between two enormous rocks. He knelt down and looked at it with amazement. There was no water for miles, and the heat was brutal.

A nomad who was passing by stopped beside him. “Everyone is surprised by that plant,” he said. “Do you know its story?”

“Please tell me,” said the traveller.

“Years ago, a seed fell here during a rare storm,” said the nomad. “It had only a few drops of water, which was enough for a tiny root. For months, it grew downward, not upward. The root searched for deep water, ignoring the scorching surface. Only when it had found moisture did a small shoot appear.”

The traveller looked at the plant again. It was thin and humble, but alive.

“Most people want to grow upward immediately,” said the nomad. “They want success and recognition fast. But in difficult places, the ones who survive are those who first build deep roots.”

The traveller thought about his own life. He had always rushed to show results, but he had never asked what supported him from below. That evening, as the sun set over the dunes, he decided to spend less time impressing others and more time strengthening himself.

Moral: In hard times, growth begins underground, so build deep roots before you reach for the sky.

title: The Weight of Words
description: A young man once approached a wise elder and confessed, “I said some terrible things about my friend.
text:
A young man once approached a wise elder and confessed, “I said some terrible things about my friend. I was angry, and now I regret it. Can I take them back?”

The elder said nothing. He picked up a pillow, cut it open and walked with the young man to the top of a hill. “Shake out the feathers,” he said.

The young man did as he was told. The wind caught the feathers, and they scattered in every direction, across the fields, over the roofs and into the distance.

“Now,” said the elder, “go and collect them all.”

“That’s impossible!” cried the young man. “They’ve gone everywhere!”

“Yes,” said the elder. “Words are the same. Once spoken, they spread beyond our reach. We may apologise, and we should, but we can never gather them all back.”

The young man stared at the empty pillow. His eyes were wet. “What should I do?”

“First, go and apologise sincerely. Then, in the future, remember the feathers before you speak. Words are easy to release but impossible to retrieve.”

The young man went to his friend, humbly asked for forgiveness and received it. From that day, he paused before every difficult sentence and asked himself whether he was ready to watch it fly.

Moral: Speak carefully, because spoken words can never be fully taken back.

title: The Boy and the Sea of Questions
description: A curious boy named Idris asked questions constantly.
text:
A curious boy named Idris asked questions constantly. “Why is the sky blue? Where does the wind go? Why do people sleep?” His teachers found him tiring, and his classmates found him strange.

One afternoon, his teacher snapped: “Idris, a sensible person doesn’t ask so many questions. Be quiet and learn what you are told!”

The boy fell silent for a week. He became pale and unhappy. His grandmother noticed and asked what was wrong.

“Teacher says that questions are foolish,” he whispered.

His grandmother smiled gently. “Do you know why you can read, why we have light in our houses and why doctors can heal the sick?” she asked. “Every single one of those things started with somebody who was brave enough to ask a foolish question.”

She gave him a small notebook. “Write your questions here. Some you’ll answer one day, and some will lead you to other questions. Never be ashamed of being curious.”

Idris filled that notebook, then another. Years later, as a scientist, he made an important discovery about water purification. At the ceremony, he thanked his grandmother and held up his first notebook.

“The answer began with a question,” he said. “And the question began with someone who told me it was all right to ask.”

Moral: Curiosity is the engine of every discovery, so never let anyone silence your questions.

title: The Sound of the Violin Maker
description: A violin maker spent his entire life seeking the perfect tone.
text:
A violin maker spent his entire life seeking the perfect tone. His instruments were admired across the country, but he himself was never satisfied.

One day, a young musician visited his workshop. “Master,” he said, “your violins are the finest I have ever heard. Yet people say you’re unhappy. Why?”

The old man took a violin from the wall and played one long note. “Listen,” he said. “What do you hear?”

“A beautiful sound,” said the musician.

“I hear every small imperfection,” he said. “For fifty years, I have chased something that does not exist: a flawless sound. And in doing so, I have missed the joy of the music itself.”

The musician was quiet. Then he took the violin and played a simple folk melody. It was slightly imperfect, but it carried such warmth that the old maker’s eyes filled with tears.

“That,” he whispered, “is what I forgot. Perfection is a technical idea. Beauty is a human one.”

After that day, the violin maker still worked with great care, but he stopped listening for flaws. Instead, he listened to what the instruments made people feel. In his final years, he was known not as the man with the perfect violins, but as the man whose violins made people cry with happiness.

Moral: Chasing perfection can rob us of joy, while embracing imperfection helps us find beauty.

title: The Thief and the Teacher
description: One night, a thief climbed into the house of a famous teacher and began to search for valuables.
text:
One night, a thief climbed into the house of a famous teacher and began to search for valuables. To his disappointment, the house was nearly empty. The teacher, who had been awake, noticed him.

“I’m sorry you didn’t find anything,” he said calmly. “Please, take my coat. It’s winter, and I wouldn’t want you to leave empty-handed.”

The thief, startled, took the coat and ran off, bewildered.

The teacher sat by the window and looked at the moon. “Poor man,” he thought. “I wish I could have given him this beautiful view as well.”

A few days later, the thief was caught and brought before a judge. The coat was identified as the teacher’s, so the teacher was summoned to testify.

“I gave him the coat,” said the teacher. “He did not steal it.”

The thief was freed, but the experience stayed with him. He couldn’t forget the teacher’s kindness, nor his own shame. Some weeks later, he knocked on the teacher’s door and asked to become his student.

He studied for years, and he eventually became one of the most respected people in the region. When people asked how he found his path, he always said, “A man gave me his coat, and I realised how little I had given anyone in my life.”

Moral: Unexpected kindness can change a person more deeply than punishment ever could.

title: The Merchant of Silence
description: In a noisy city, there lived a man who claimed to sell silence.
text:
In a noisy city, there lived a man who claimed to sell silence. People laughed at his small stall, with its sign: “Silence for Sale. One Hour, One Coin.”

A restless businessman, curious and weary, decided to try. He paid his coin and sat down on a plain wooden bench in a quiet garden behind the stall. “Is that it?” he asked.

“That’s it,” said the merchant. “For one hour, you may not speak, read or use your phone. You only sit.”

At first, the businessman felt ridiculous. His mind raced. He thought about emails, deadlines and arguments. After twenty minutes, he wanted to leave. But the merchant’s calm eyes stopped him.

Gradually, his thoughts slowed down. He began to hear birds, the wind in the leaves and his own breathing. Things that had troubled him for months seemed to dissolve. By the end of the hour, he saw a solution to a problem that had kept him awake for weeks.

When he stood up, his shoulders felt lighter. “I paid for nothing,” he said with astonishment, “yet I received more than I’ve ever bought.”

The merchant bowed. “People spend fortunes on noise,” he said, “and are surprised when they feel empty.”

The businessman returned every week afterwards, and soon he brought his employees along.

Moral: In a world full of noise, silence may be the most valuable thing we can give ourselves.

title: The Apprentice and the Mirror
description: A master potter took on a talented but arrogant apprentice named Lina.
text:
A master potter took on a talented but arrogant apprentice named Lina. She learned quickly, and after a year, she thought she knew everything.

“Your teaching has become unnecessary,” she told her master. “My pots are as good as yours.”

The master said nothing. He took one of her finest bowls and one of his own and placed them side by side on the table. “Which is better?” he asked.

Lina inspected them and, to her surprise, couldn’t decide. They looked almost identical.

“Now,” said the master, “fill both with water.”

She did so. Her bowl leaked slowly from a tiny crack that she hadn’t noticed. His held every drop.

“The difference between us is invisible to the eye,” said the master. “It’s in the details, in the thousand small decisions you make when nobody is looking. That is not something you can learn in a year. It takes a lifetime.”

Lina stared at the puddle. Her pride had blinded her to something simple: being good isn’t the same as being excellent.

She stayed another ten years. When she finally opened her own workshop, she hung a small mirror above the door. Underneath it, she wrote: “Look carefully before you say you’re finished.”

Moral: Excellence lies in the small details that nobody notices, and humility keeps us learning.

title: The Lantern Seller
description: In a town at the foot of a mountain, a lantern seller named Omar had a shop that was always busy during the long winter nights.
text:
In a town at the foot of a mountain, a lantern seller named Omar had a shop that was always busy during the long winter nights. His lanterns were sturdy and bright, and travellers praised them.

One evening, a strange customer entered. He was a blind man, led by a dog. “I’d like to buy your best lantern,” he said.

Omar was puzzled. “Forgive me, sir, but why would a blind man need a lantern?”

The man smiled. “Because of other people. When I walk in the dark with a lantern, others can see me and avoid walking into me. My light is not for my own eyes. It’s a gift to everyone on the road.”

Omar was deeply moved. He gave the man the best lantern in the shop and refused to take any money. Afterwards, he often thought about the visitor. He had always seen his work as selling light to those who needed it, but the blind man had shown him a deeper truth: light has value when it is shared.

From then on, Omar left a lantern burning outside his shop every night, so that any lonely traveller could find their way, even without making a purchase. Strangely, his business doubled.

Moral: The light we carry helps not only ourselves but everyone who walks near us.

title: The Wise Fool
description: In the court of an old king lived a man called the Fool.
text:
In the court of an old king lived a man called the Fool. He wore bright clothes and made everybody laugh, but he was cleverer than the ministers.

One day, the king gave him a golden staff and said, “Keep this until you find someone who is a bigger fool than you. Then give it to him.”

Years passed. The Fool carried the staff everywhere. Eventually, the king fell gravely ill. The Fool visited him and found him very weak.

“I am going on a long journey,” said the king in a faint voice.

“When will you return?” asked the Fool.

“I will never return.”

“Have you prepared for it? Have you sent servants ahead? Have you packed your possessions?”

“No,” whispered the king. “Nothing can be taken with me. I will go alone.”

The Fool stood up and placed the golden staff in the king’s hands. “Then this belongs to you,” he said. “I have met many people who worried about small things, but you are the greatest fool of all. You spent your whole life collecting treasures, and you never thought about the one journey that really matters.”

The king looked at the staff and began to weep, but his tears were not of anger. In his final days, he gave away much of his wealth and made peace with his enemies.

Moral: Don’t spend your whole life preparing for everything except what truly matters.

title: The Stonecutter
description: A stonecutter spent his days chipping rocks from a mountain.
text:
A stonecutter spent his days chipping rocks from a mountain. It was heavy, boring work, and he often complained. “If only I were rich,” he muttered, “life would be so much easier.”

One day, a mountain spirit heard him. “Your wish is granted,” it said. In an instant, the stonecutter became a wealthy merchant, living in a splendid house.

He was delighted, until he saw a prince riding by with a hundred servants. “The prince has far more power than I do,” he thought. “If only I were a prince!” At once, he became one.

But as a prince, he suffered from the heat of the sun. “The sun is stronger than any king,” he said. “I wish I were the sun.” And so he became the sun, burning brightly in the sky.

Soon a cloud drifted across and blocked his light. “The cloud is mightier than I am!” he cried, and became a cloud. But the wind pushed him around the sky. So he became the wind, which was stopped only by a giant mountain that never moved.

“The mountain is the strongest of all,” he said. “I wish I were a mountain!”

At last, he was a mountain, enormous and unmovable. But he felt a sharp pain in his side. A small man with a hammer was chipping away at his stone. It was a stonecutter.

For the first time, the former stonecutter understood.

Moral: Envy blinds us to our own value, and happiness starts with appreciating who we are.

title: The Last Apple
description: During a long and bitter winter, a village ran short of food.
text:
During a long and bitter winter, a village ran short of food. Families shared what little they had, but the snow lay so deep that nobody could travel to the market.

In one cottage lived an old widow with a single apple left in her pantry. She looked at it for a long time. Her stomach ached with hunger, but she thought of her neighbour, a young mother with three small children, who had almost nothing.

Quietly, she wrapped the apple in a cloth and left it on the mother’s doorstep before dawn.

The young mother woke up and found the gift, and her eyes filled with tears. But she, too, remembered an elderly man down the road who lived alone and hadn’t been seen for days. She cut the apple into thin slices, kept one for each child and took the remaining pieces to the old man.

The old man, deeply moved, remembered that his sick sister lived at the end of the village. He shared his slice with her and gave the rest to a passing shepherd.

By evening, the shepherd returned to the widow’s cottage, seeking shelter from the storm. “Somebody left me a piece of apple today,” he said. “It was the best thing I’ve ever tasted. Please come and eat with me. I have a sheep, and I’d like to share it.”

Because of one small act, the whole village had food that night.

Moral: Generosity spreads like warmth, and one small gift can feed many.

title: The Interpreter's Mistake
description: A young interpreter named Marco was hired to translate at an important business negotiation between two companies from different countries.
text:
A young interpreter named Marco was hired to translate at an important business negotiation between two companies from different countries. He was confident and well prepared.

During the second hour, one executive said a sentence that contained a delicate phrase. Marco realised, with a sinking feeling, that the literal translation might sound insulting in the other language. He had two choices: translate it word for word and risk offending everybody, or soften it and risk being accused of changing the message.

He decided on a third option. He paused and spoke honestly. “Excuse me, I need to clarify something. The phrase that was just used has a different tone in your language. What the speaker means is, ‘We have serious concerns, but we respect your proposal.’ Would you like me to translate it exactly, or explain the intention?”

The room went quiet. Then the foreign delegate smiled. “Please explain the intention. Thank you for your honesty.”

The negotiation continued smoothly. Afterwards, the older executive approached him. “Most interpreters would have been afraid to stop the meeting,” he said. “But a bridge between two languages is only valuable if it carries meaning, not just words.”

From that day, Marco’s reputation grew. He became known as the interpreter who protected understanding rather than his own pride.

Moral: Real communication is about meaning, and sometimes it takes courage to pause and clarify.

title: The Tightrope Walker
description: A famous tightrope walker once stretched a rope across a deep gorge, high above a roaring river.
text:
A famous tightrope walker once stretched a rope across a deep gorge, high above a roaring river. A huge crowd gathered to watch.

He crossed without trouble, then returned, and the audience cheered. Next, he pushed a wheelbarrow across, and the crowd roared even louder.

Then he turned to the spectators. “Do you believe I can carry a person across in this wheelbarrow?”

“Yes!” everybody shouted. “You are the greatest!”

“Do you truly believe it?” he asked.

“Absolutely!”

“Then,” he said, pointing at a man in the front row, “please climb in.”

The man went pale. He stepped backwards and shook his head. Suddenly, the whole crowd was silent. Nobody moved.

The tightrope walker smiled. “This is the difference between belief and trust,” he said. “Belief is easy when it costs nothing. Trust means putting yourself in the wheelbarrow.”

At last, a small boy pushed through the crowd. “I’ll go,” he said. “My father trusts you, and I trust my father.”

The boy sat in the wheelbarrow, and together they crossed the gorge slowly, with the entire crowd holding its breath. When they arrived safely on the other side, the cheering lasted for minutes.

Moral: Real faith is not what we say, but what we are willing to risk.

title: The Mapmaker
description: In a mountainous kingdom lived a mapmaker named Isolde, who was famous for the beauty of her maps.
text:
In a mountainous kingdom lived a mapmaker named Isolde, who was famous for the beauty of her maps. Every river was drawn in delicate blue, and every forest was shaded in rich green.

One day, a young explorer bought one of her maps and set off across the mountains. Within days, he was lost. The map showed a bridge that no longer existed and a road that had been washed away years earlier. Furious, he returned to her workshop.

“Your map almost killed me!” he said. “It’s beautiful but useless.”

Isolde examined it and sighed. “I drew this twenty years ago,” she said. “At the time, it was accurate.”

“Then why do you still sell it?”

She hesitated. “Because I’m proud of how it looks. I never checked whether it still matched the land.”

The explorer’s anger faded. “Maybe that is true of more than maps,” he said. “Many people go through life using an old picture of the world, though it has changed completely.”

Isolde nodded slowly. That night, she burned her old maps. In the morning, she packed her instruments and walked into the mountains herself, measuring every path with her own eyes. Her new maps were plainer and less decorated, but they were true. Travellers trusted them with their lives.

Moral: Never mistake a beautiful, outdated picture for reality. Check it against the world.

title: The Chessboard and the Rice
description: According to an old legend, a clever courtier once invented a new game and presented it to his king.
text:
According to an old legend, a clever courtier once invented a new game and presented it to his king. The king loved it so much that he offered the inventor any reward he wished.

“Your Majesty,” said the courtier humbly, “I ask for something very small. Place one grain of rice on the first square of the chessboard, two on the second, four on the third, and continue doubling for each of the sixty-four squares.”

The king laughed. “Is that all? A man of your talent could have asked for gold or land!” He ordered his servants to prepare the rice.

At first, the numbers looked trivial. By the tenth square, there were only five hundred grains. By the twentieth, about half a million, still just a few sacks. The king was amused.

But by the thirtieth square, the amount had grown to over a billion grains. By the fortieth, it filled granaries. By the sixty-fourth, the total was so large that no kingdom on earth could have provided it. It was more than all the rice ever grown in history.

The king fell silent. He had not understood how quickly small, steady increases could accumulate when they multiplied. He had underestimated the power of exponential growth.

He admired the courtier’s intelligence, and appointed him chief advisor, instead of demanding the impossible reward.

Moral: Small things that grow steadily can become unimaginably powerful.

title: The Donkey in the Well
description: A farmer’s old donkey fell into a deep, dry well.
text:
A farmer’s old donkey fell into a deep, dry well. The animal cried out in distress for hours while the farmer paced around the edge, wondering what to do.

He eventually concluded that the donkey was too old to be worth saving, and the well was already useless and overdue for filling in. He called his neighbours, and together they began shovelling earth into the well to bury both problems at once.

At first, the donkey panicked. But gradually, as the dirt landed on its back, it noticed something. Each time a load of earth fell on it, it shook the dirt off and stepped up onto the new layer.

“Shake it off and step up,” it repeated to itself. “Shake it off and step up.”

The neighbours kept shovelling, and the donkey kept climbing. The pile beneath its feet grew higher and higher, until finally, exhausted but unharmed, the donkey stepped over the edge of the well and trotted away.

The farmer and his neighbours stared in astonishment.

What had been intended to bury the donkey had become the very thing that saved it.

When the farmer later told the story in the village, an old woman nodded. “Life will often throw dirt at you,” she said. “If you let it pile up on your back, you’ll be buried. But if you shake it off and use it as a step, even your troubles can lift you higher.”

Moral: Every problem can become a stepping stone if we refuse to be buried by it.

title: The Price of an Hour
description: A successful lawyer came home late every evening, exhausted and irritable.
text:
A successful lawyer came home late every evening, exhausted and irritable. One night, his five-year-old son was waiting for him at the door.

“Dad, can I ask you something?”

“Of course,” said the lawyer, loosening his tie. “What is it?”

“How much money do you earn in an hour?”

The lawyer frowned. It seemed an odd question, and he was tired. “That’s none of your business. Why do you ask?”

“I just want to know. Please tell me.”

“Fine,” said the lawyer. “About two hundred dollars.”

The boy looked at the floor. Then he ran upstairs and came back with his piggy bank. He emptied it onto the carpet and counted carefully. “I have a hundred and twenty dollars,” he said. “I need eighty more. Could you lend it to me?”

The lawyer was about to lecture him about wasting money, but something in the boy’s expression stopped him.

“What do you want to buy?” he asked quietly.

“Nothing,” said the boy. “I want to buy one hour of your time. I have saved the money, and I would like to spend that hour with you.”

The lawyer felt his throat tighten. He pulled his son into his arms and said nothing for a long time. The next morning, he cancelled his meetings and took the day off.

Moral: Time spent with the people we love is the one investment we can never recover.

title: The Monk and the River
description: Two monks were travelling together when they reached a shallow river.
text:
Two monks were travelling together when they reached a shallow river. A young woman in an elegant dress stood on the bank, unable to cross without ruining her clothes and, worse, losing her footing in the current.

Without a word, the older monk lifted her onto his shoulders, carried her across and set her down gently on the other side. She thanked him warmly, and the monks continued on their way.

The younger monk, however, grew increasingly uneasy. They had been taught to avoid contact with women, and he could not understand his companion’s behaviour. For an hour, he walked in silence, his irritation growing with every step.

Finally, he could bear it no longer. “How could you do that?” he burst out. “You broke our vows! You carried that woman as if it were nothing!”

The older monk looked at him calmly. “I left her by the river two hours ago,” he said. “Are you still carrying her?”

The younger monk fell silent. He suddenly realised that while his companion had done a simple act of kindness and moved on, he himself had spent two hours turning the moment over in his mind, building resentment out of a single gesture.

They walked on without speaking, but the younger monk’s step had become lighter.

Moral: Don’t carry yesterday’s moments into today. Let them go.

title: The Butterfly's Struggle
description: One spring morning, a boy found a cocoon hanging from a branch in his garden.
text:
One spring morning, a boy found a cocoon hanging from a branch in his garden. A small opening had appeared, and he sat nearby for hours, watching a butterfly struggle to push its body through the tiny hole.

The creature seemed exhausted. Several times it stopped moving altogether, as if it had given up. The boy felt sorry for it. “It’s suffering,” he thought. “Surely I can make this easier.”

He fetched a pair of scissors and carefully cut the edge of the cocoon. The butterfly tumbled out almost immediately. Its body was swollen, and its wings were small and crumpled.

The boy waited for the wings to unfold and strengthen, but nothing happened. The butterfly crawled around the branch, unable to fly. It lived only a few days.

Confused, the boy told his grandfather what had happened. The old man sighed. “You meant well,” he said, “but you didn’t understand. The struggle through that narrow opening forces fluid from the body into the wings. Without it, the wings never develop properly. What looked like suffering was actually preparation.”

“So I harmed it by helping?” asked the boy.

“You harmed it by rescuing it from something it needed,” said his grandfather gently. “There is a difference between supporting someone and removing every obstacle from their path.”

The boy never forgot that lesson. Years later, as a father, he resisted the urge to solve every problem for his children. He stood nearby, ready to support them, but he let them push through the narrow places on their own.

Moral: Struggle is sometimes the very thing that gives us the strength to fly.

title: The Second Arrow
description: A young monk named Tenzin was struggling with a bitter disappointment.
text:
A young monk named Tenzin was struggling with a bitter disappointment. He had spent two years preparing for an important teaching role, but the position was given to someone else. For weeks, he could neither eat nor sleep properly.

He went to his master and poured out his frustration. “I was treated unfairly,” he said. “I keep replaying the moment in my mind, and I feel worse every day.”

The master listened patiently. “When a person is struck by an arrow, he feels pain,” he said. “That is unavoidable. But if a second arrow hits him in exactly the same spot, the pain doubles. Do you know who fires the second arrow?”

Tenzin shook his head.

“He does it himself,” said the master. “The first arrow is the event: the lost position. The second arrow is everything you tell yourself afterwards: ‘I’m not good enough,’ ‘it’s always like this,’ ‘my life is ruined.’ Nobody forces you to fire it.”

Tenzin lowered his eyes. He realised that most of his suffering had come from his own thoughts, not from the decision itself.

“Does this mean I shouldn’t feel anything?” he asked.

“Not at all,” replied the master. “Feel the first arrow honestly. Grieve if you must. But once the pain has been acknowledged, put your bow down.”

That evening, Tenzin sat in the garden and, for the first time in weeks, simply let the sadness exist without arguing with it. By morning, it had lost much of its sting.

Moral: We cannot avoid every misfortune, but we can refuse to multiply it with our own thoughts.
